items.stem: Why can piping into a while-read loop lose variable changes in some shells?

options.text: The piped loop runs in a subshell whose variable changes do not propagate to the parent
options.rationale: A pipeline segment runs in a subshell; its variable mutations are local to it.
read -r preserves backslashes; it does not lose state.
They can; the issue is subshell scope.

options.text: The loop never executes when piped
options.rationale: It executes, but in a subshell.

items.stem: Select TWO practices that make a shell script more robust.

options.text: Enabling set -euo pipefail at the top
options.rationale: Strict mode surfaces errors, unset variables and pipeline failures early.

options.text: Using read -r to avoid mangling backslashes
options.rationale: -r stops read from interpreting backslash escapes.

options.text: Parsing filenames by splitting command output with for on whitespace
options.rationale: That breaks on spaces and newlines in names.

options.text: Relying on bashisms when the shebang is /bin/sh
options.rationale: That breaks portability under a POSIX shell.

items.explanation: Strict mode surfaces errors, unset variables and pipeline failures early.

items.stem: What is the purpose of wait after launching background jobs with &?

options.text: It blocks until the specified (or all) background jobs finish before continuing
options.rationale: wait synchronises the script with its background children.

options.text: It kills all background jobs immediately
options.rationale: wait waits for completion; it does not kill.

options.text: It runs the next command in the background

options.rationale: wait does not disable job control.

items.explanation: wait synchronises the script with its background children.
